blocks.x: THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION
Oral History
Interview with Quinn Wilson by Don DeMichael
Part 1
December 3, 1977

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
P R O C E E D I N G S
Why don't you --
Okay, Quinn Wilson, 2323 Dempster, Evanston, Illinois.
All Right. You were born here, in Chicago?
Yeah.
When was that?
December 26th, 1908.
Where at?
Out in Englewood, Illinois, really. 61st and N. ?
Oh, yeah. Well, that's part of the --
(Simultaneous conversation, unintelligible.)
Englewood, yeah.
When did you first get interested in music?

Well, it's kind of funny situation. We had an old violin sitting in the corner, and my mother figured she didn't know what to do with it, and my uncle left it there. So she figured she'd give me violin lessons, and if I did all right, why she'd keep it up. So we got ahold of a violin teacher, I don't know how we got in touch with him, Mr. Stanbourn (PHONETIC), but he was a good violin teacher. He was a German.
Stanbourn?
Yeah, Lewis Stanborn.
Sanborn?
Yeah, Lewis Sanborn. So I started taking lessons from him, and I did so well, they kept it up.
How old were you then, Quinn?
Ten years old.
Ten years old. Was anyone besides your uncle musical, that you know of, in your family?
Not that I know of. I had -- my uncle played drums. Played what they called trap drums.
The same uncle that had the violin?
No, this was another uncle.
Uh-huh. Did he play professionally?
Yeah. So far as I know.
In Chicago?
No, in Jackson, Mississippi.
Is that where your family's from?
That's where my family's from, yeah.
But you were born here?
I was born in Chicago, yeah.
When did your family come to Chicago, do you know?
Oh, I don't know exactly. My father came to Chicago when he was six years old, and that was just
So you're really a long generation Chicagoan?
Right.
Well, your teacher, Mr. Sanborn, did he teach you the classical literature?
Yes. Oh, yeah, I was into concertos, and everything. I took harmony and theory.
And this is all before you went to high school?
This is all before I went to high school, yeah. I was still in the grade school.
Where did you take your lessons at?
He came to the house.
Oh, I see. A visiting --
Yes.
-- music professor. How long did you study?
Oooooohh! I studied until I got in the high school.
What high school did you go to?
Wendell Phillips
Wendell Phillips High? A lot of good musicians come out of Wendell Phillips.
That's right.
Yeah. Did it have a reputation for good musical training then? When was this? About 19 --
About 1923.
Did Wendell Phillips have a reputation as being a good place to study music then?
Yes, we had it then. We had a good musical department. We had an orchestra and we had a band, ROTC band.
Uh-huh. Were you in the ROTC --
That's how I got into the tuba.
Oh, yeah? Tell me about that.
When I started in Phillips High School, a friend of mine belonged to the ROTC band, and I wanted to get in the band. So his name was Charlie Allen.
The trumpet player?
Trumpet player, that's right.
Mouthpiece maker.

Mouthpiece maker. So he wanted to know if I -- what instrument I wanted to play. So I couldn't think of nothing else but the bass drums. And he said, 'oh, no.' Said, 'You don't want -- how you going to play bass drum? You can only play bass drum in one band, that's like a military band.'

So I said, 'Well, you got it.' So he went upstairs and come downstairs with an old, beat-up tuba, and handed it to me. So I said, 'What can I do with this, Charlie?' I said, 'this has only got three valves. I play violin with seven positions.' He said, 'That's all right, don't worry about it. I'll teach you.' So he taught me the fingering.
Well, was Charlie a student then, or --
Yeah, he was a student.
Uh-huh. Who was the band director?
In fact, he was in his senior year, then.
When you were a freshman?
Yeah.
Who was the band director?
I'm trying to think of it. I can't think of his first name. His last name was Hanson, Captain Hanson.
Captain Hanson. Is that the school that Walter Dyett taught at later?
Later. In later years, yeah.
Gene Ammons went there?
Gene Ammons went there.
All those guys.
Yeah.
Well, obviously you learned tuba.
How long did it take you to get into the band?
Well, I don't know. I'd say about a month.
Uh-huh. Were you in the band all through high school?

All through high school. In fact, after the first semester, Charlie Allen was graduated. He was a 2nd Lieutenant. The 1st Lieutenant, the doctor took him off his instrument, on account of his health, and the captain graduated. And I wound up being captain of the band in one semester.
Really?
Uh-huh.
The captain in the ROTC? You had the uniform and everything like that?
Yeah.
Why did you want to get into the ROTC?
Well, it wasn't exactly the ROTC there, I just wanted to get into the band. I just wanted some instrument beside the violin.
Were you tired of the violin by then?
I wasn't tired of it, because I was still playing violin in the orchestra, school orchestra.
You were in both the band and the orchestra?
Yeah, band and the orchestra. Yeah.
I see. Well, did you start playing professionally when you were in high school?
Yes.
Tell me about that.
Well, there's one reason why I didn't finish school. A friend of mine heard me on tuba, and he recommended me to a band leader that had a orchestra.
Who was the friend? Was he a musician?
Yeah, he turned out to be -- later years he turned out to be my brother-in-law, name of Jimmy MacEndry. (PHONETIC).
I see.
He was the drummer in the band.
In the professional band?
In the professional band. So I started playing with them when I was in high school, and in the meantime.
What was the name of the band, do you recall?
The name of the band was -- what was his name? Henderson
Hennessey?
No, Henderson.
Henderson. Like Fletcher Henderson?
Yeah, like Fletcher, but -- Monroe Henderson. No, it wasn't Monroe, either. It was -- Monroe Richardson.
Richardson was the name of the band?
The name of the band.
How big a band was it?
It was about nine pieces.
Was -- would we have called it a jazz band, now?

Yes. See, back in those days they had what they called jazz bands, Creole jazz bands. And then they had white bands that played in ballrooms. We was playing opposite the white bands in Midway Gardens.
I see.
It's 60th and Cottage Grove.
When was this?
That was about 1925.
1925. You would have been 17?
Yeah.
About 17.
Just about.
Was it a regular gig, you know?
Yeah, well, on weekends. Like Friday, Saturday, and Sunday.
Uh-huh. And you played for dancing?
Yeah. And the band we played opposite was named Art Castle.
Oh, yeah. Yeah, that's a well-known band.
Yeah.
Where was Midway Gardens?
60th and Cottage Grove. Midway, there.
Do you recall who else was in the band that you were playing with?
Not offhand.
Uh-huh. How long did you play with that band?
I played with that band, oh, I guess it was about two or three months.
And you were still going to school?
Still going to school. And then that same band was taken over by Art Simms. He played violin and we got a job up in Milwaukee. Three nights a week.
Where in Milwaukee?
At Riverside Gardens.
Riverside Gardens?
Uh-huh.
Was that the same band, had a lot of Chicago men in it? Or it was a Chicago --

It was a Chicago band. See, because they used to come by Wendell Phillips and pick me up. See, we worked Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday. They'd come by Wendell Phillips High School and pick me up Wednesday afternoon. We'd go up there and play and come back Thursday morning and go to school Friday and Saturday, then they'd pick me up Saturday afternoon, then we'd go up and play Saturday and Sunday, and then bring me back Monday morning.
Do you remember who was in Art Simms' band?
One, I remember the trombone player, Preston Jackson.
Preston Jackson. Was Zilber Randolph in that band?
Later.
Later. That was after you --
After ART died, yeah. No, he was in the same time I was. See, Art Simms died, and Bernie Young took it over.
Right. Bernie Young's band.
Bernie Young's band.
That's a well-known band. They never recorded.
Never -- no, I don't think so.
But I've read about it. And I interviewed Zilmer Randolph on the same project that I'm doing you. And he was telling me about that band, said it was really a good band.
It was. Yes, it was.
Well, how long were you with that band?

I stayed with that band about six months. Then I left and gigged around Chicago for a little while, and then I went back with Art Simms. When I went back with Art Simms is when he died. And I stayed with Bernie Young, oh, I guess for about -- almost a year.
Did you go with Erskine Tate after Bernie Young?
No. See, I went with Walter Barnes, at the Arcadia Ballroom on Broadway.
That's up north, here?
Up north, yeah, on Broadway.
Now, who was he?
Walter Barnes? What did Walter Barnes play? He was the band that got burn up in Natchez, Mississippi. You remember that?
No. When was that?

Well, I was still -- I was with Earl Hines, then. This was back in the thirties. They got trapped in a dance. I worked with him for a little while, and then Erskine Tate heard about me. And he wanted me to come with his band. So that's the reason I had to get on the bass fiddle. Because this was playing for silent pictures in the moving picture theater pit.
Now, with all the other bands you'd been playing tuba. And they had arrangements? It wasn't, you know, a "fake" band?
Oh, no, no. We had --
Everything was written.
Yeah, we had things written.
Okay, now. Tate was playing -- what theater was he playing at?
AT the Metropolitan Theater and the Vendome Theater.
Doubling?
Yeah.
But what did you do?

Well, during that time, that was during the time they was changing over from silent pictures to talkies, see. Like on Sundays they'd have talking pictures at the Metropolitan Theater, and then during the week they'd have silent pictures at the Vendome, so we'd go down and play
for the silent pictures in the Vendome Theater.
How big a band did Tate have?
Twelve pieces.
Twelve pieces. And that's when you switched to string bass?
That's when I switched to string bass.
Did you find that difficult?

No, I had about two weeks to learn it. Because back in them days we only gave two weeks notice. You didn't have to give a four weeks notice. So what we did, the bass player that was with Walter Barnes went with Erskine Tate, and I went with Erskine Tate. And -- no, Walter Barnes' bass player, we switched jobs.
I see. He was with --
He was with Walter Barnes. He went -- I went with Tate, and then he went with Walter Barnes. That's what it was.
What was his name?
I forgot.
He didn't like working with Tate?
No, we switched jobs because Tate wanted me. So we just changed jobs.
What sort of music did you play with Tate?
Like I say, we played for silent

pictures. Played all kinds, played jazz, classical, overtures, and quite naturally, we had to play for the pictures, so we had to play -- they sent out a release -- when they sent a picture out during the week, they'd send a score with it. And you had to have all these different numbers in the score in order to play for the picture. Because the librarian, he'd see-me to work early and watch the picture and watch the score and set up the numbers. And then when we'd come to work, we had to set up the numbers according to the picture.
You mean the arrangements?
The arrangements, yeah.
And you'd have to go from one to the other?
One to the other, and you didn't get a chance to play a full one. Sometimes you didn't get a chance to play but two or three bars.
That was pretty hard work.
Oh, yes it was. But it's real fascinating for a young fellow.
(Laughter.)
(Inaudible).

Yeah, had to watch the conductor, see, because you had -- like you'd have a five finger theme, four finger theme, two finger theme. And he watched the picture, and the minute the scene changes, he'd cut the band off. You'd be right in the middle. Then he'd hold up five fingers, and

then you'd go to your five finger theme. Thumb theme, he'd hold up a thumb. You go to the thumb theme. You had music all over your rack. So you could grab it at a moment's notice, see. Then he'd take the stick and cut the band off. You had to cut. Then he'd hold up his five fingers, and you'd go pick that up, put it in, and he'd start off and you'd start playing that for a little while. Then maybe there's a big fight coming, or something. Cut. Then you go into your hurry, what you call hurry, hurry number one, two, number three, number four, number five.
Like a gallop.
The gallop, yeah. Oh, it was real fascinating.
And these were hand signals?
Yeah, the conductor, you know.
Or numbers of the parts.
Uh-huh.
Well, did you play in the pit? Well, sure, you would play in the pit for the movies. Did you also play on the stage?
Well, that was when I went to the Regal. That was later.
Uh-huh. But Tate's band --
Tate's band, we only had -- we didn't have a stage.
I see. Because he's fairly well-known, you know, as a theater band.
Yeah. Well, we had to do our O's and everything from the pit.
You had to do what?
We had to do the overture, and everything, from the pit.
I see. Do you recall who was in Tate's band at this time?
Oh --
And when was this, about 19 --
This was in 1928.
1928 when I started with Tate.
I see. Well, can we back up a little bit? Who were you playing with when you made the records with Jelly Roll?
That was in between engagements, but Art Simms, in Milwaukee. Because I wasn't working.
You were about 18 at that time?
Yeah.
19, something like that.
Something like that.
Did you work with Jelly on anything other than the recordings?
No.

Tell me about him. There's been a lot of stories about him, how he would put the band together, and being somewhat of an odd character. In later years he bragged about, you know, coming up from New Orleans, and so on, showing the Chicago guys a thing or two, because he bragged a lot. But what kind of guy was he?
Well, I found him to be very nice. I never had any problems with him.
How did he call you --
He called me -- I don't know how he happened to call me for that record session. I don't know who recommended me to him.
Dodds Brothers were on that?
Yeah.
And George Mitchell?
George Mitchell.
And one of the --
Kid Ory on trombone.
I think one of the Reeves Brothers (PHONETIC) was on --
Some of them, yeah.
Ruben Reeves?
Ruben Reeves, yeah.
On trombone?
Yeah. We had different personnel on -- I made about ten sides with Jelly.
Yeah, I was looking at two sections last night, the one where he made "Wild Man" and "Jungle Blues", and --
Yeah.
And one of my favorite Jelly compositions, "The Pearls."
Yeah, that's my -- that was my favorite. You'd be surprised, that's probably the only one I really remember out of the whole session, "The Pearls." Oh, man. Yeah.
Yeah, well, that was a piano piece, originally. How did he -- did he write out the music, or did he just sing the part?
Yeah, he wrote it. He wrote the music, yeah.
He wrote out the music for all the horns?
For all the horns.
Well, how did he rehearse the band? Did you rehearse in the studios, or someplace else?
In the studio. For -- you know, during the session.
Yeah. Well, how did he -- how did
he work?

Well, he just -- when you started rehearsing, we just rehearsed the first tune we were going to record. We'd run it down, and rehearse it and get it down, timing and everything. And after we got it down, we'd just go ahead and record it.
Stump Evans was in that -- on that recording date. Alto player?
Yeah.
Was his name Stump or Stomp? I've seen it both ways.
Now, you know, I don't remember. Because we always called him Stump.
Stump?
Yeah.
Sometimes he's referred to as Stomp Evans.
Yeah. I've heard Stump.
Stump, was he a short man, or --
Yeah. Yeah, he was short.
The ensembles on these records, I was listening to them again last night. Parts of it sound like there are two trumpets. Was there just the one trumpet?
It could have been, what's the name,
Clay?
Shirley Clay?
Shirley Clay, and Joyce could have been on the record.
Uh-huh. Why do you say they could have been?
You say it sound like two trumpets.
Yeah. But why do you say Shirley Clay might have been?
Because I know he made some of the sessions with us.
He made some of the sessions with you?
Yeah, he, Shirley Clay, yeah.
And Jelly?
Yeah.
One of the sessions the band -- the session that you recorded "The Pearls," according to the discographies, that was the same date that Jelly made a couple of trio sides with Johnny and Baby Dodds?
Uh-huh.
Were you there when they made that?
Yeah, I was there.
I mean, did he just say, I want to do this trio thing?
Yeah.
And there are a couple of different masters available of that. And also of "Pearls" I believe. "Pearls" has two masters.
Yeah?
Yeah, there's two of "Beale Street," and there's two of the "Pearls", and two of "Wolverine Blues." That have been issued.
Yeah?

These are French records. And there's some variation, you know, on the solos and in the ensembles. It seems like some of the arrangements had loose parts in them, you know, where you didn't have to do exactly what Jelly had written or instructed you to do. Am I wrong there, or was it all very strictly controlled?
Well, except for the solos. You know, you did your own improvising on your solos.
The ensembles sound very loose, you know, these New Orleans ensembles.
Yeah, that's the way he wrote.
Did the guys have trouble reading it?
No.
What kind of man was Johnny Dodds?
Oh, he was wonderful. Nice and quiet.
What about Baby?
Baby, well, he was the same way. Told a lot of jokes.
They were both in the Oliver Band, the Oliver Creole Jazz Band.
Yeah.
Did you ever hear that band?
King Oliver?
The King Oliver Jazz --
Yes.
Where, at Lincoln Gardens?
No, I heard them when they was at the Mahjong, across the street from Sunset.
Did you ever play with Oliver?
No, I never worked with Oliver.

Did you work -- well, let me -- some people have done some research, and have looked up old columns that were written by one of the big band leaders on Southside in the twenties, Dave Peyton, maybe, wrote a column for The Defender.
"Defender", right.

And it seems like there were like three divisions of musicians on the Southside, those who played in the theaters, and those who played in ballrooms, and those who played in what they called cabarets. And some

of his columns, he puts down the guys who were playing in cabarets, a lot of the New Orleans musicians. There seemed to be some bad feeling between the established Chicago musicians and the guys coming up from New Orleans. Were you aware of any of that?
No, I wasn't. I worked with Dave Peyton at the Regal Theater.
When was that?
That was when I left Erskine Tate. I just came across the street to the Regal.
Well, you've worked and recorded with a lot of the musicians who came from New Orleans, like the Dodds Brothers. You worked with Jimmy Noone, I believe.
Yeah.
Did they operate differently from the guys who, you know, were from Chicago? I mean, were they harder to work for, easier to work for, or --
No, I didn't see any difference.
What was Noone's band like, at Dreamland?
Now, that band I didn't work with.
Which band did you work with, with Jimmy?
I'm trying to think now. Am I supposed to be on that band at Dreamland?
Well, I don't know.
(Unintelligible)
Well, I have here, the Apex, and then I think when I talked to you a few weeks ago you mentioned the Dreamland. Did you work --
I worked with Tiny Parham at the Dreamland.
Did you work with Jimmy Noone?
Yeah. But I didn't -- I wasn't with him very long at the Dreamland.
Uh-huh. Did he have a big band or a small band?
It was a small band.
Yeah? Do you remember who was in it?
No, I don't. The one I remember is the drummer, Zutty Singleton.
Uh-huh. Was it a fake band or a reading band?
Yeah.
Fake band?
Fake band.
At the Dreamland, did people dance there, or --
It was a cabaret.
And people danced in all the cabarets?
Yeah. And you had a little, small show.
Well, that was during Prohibition. Were they like speakeasies, or was whisky served?
Uh-huh -- no, you had to bring your own whisky and get your own set-up.
I see. What did the club do, just provide the band and --
The show.
Did they charge to get in?
Band and show. No, you had a cover. What they called a cover charge. Small cover charge, but it was just like admission.
Sure. Did they do good business?
Yeah, fine business.
All those places?
All those places did business.
Were they operated by the gangsters, or --
No, the Dreamland was operated by one man.
Who was he?
Bill Bottoms.
Bill Bottoms. Was he a white man
or black man?
Black man.
There was more than one Dreamland, weren't there two Dreamlands?
Yeah, well, that was the Dreamland Ballroom. That was on West Side.
That was different?
Yeah, that was different. See, that was a long time ago, and that was a ballroom, Dreamland Ballroom, where Charlie Cook had the band.
Did you ever work with Charlie Cook?
No.
Was there -- did the young guys sort of hang together, and the older guys hang together, back in the twenties?

Well, it's hard to say, because as I remember back in the twenties, like I was -- in most bands I was in, I was the youngest man in the band. It's not like it is nowadays with these rock bands, where you all start out together.
I see.

See, when I -- all the bands I got in, they were men. And very few young musicians, you know. All of us were scattered in different bands and wasn't but, you know, just a few of us. So I would say we hung out with the
band.
I see. Was the union strong then?
Yeah, it was pretty strong.
Did you get work through the union, or
No. Most of my contacts, I don't know, was through different people recommending me.
Same way it is today?
Same way it is today.
Well, you must have been a terror on tuba back then. You got an awful lot of work.
(Laughing) Yeah, I kept pretty busy.
Well, were you doubling tuba and bass?
Yeah, that's just when I started doubling in the Met. See, when music get too tough, you know, for the string bass, I'd jump on the tuba.
Oh, really? It was easier to read the parts on tuba?

Yeah, because, see, I was a freshman on the string bass, you know. And some of them bass parts, you know, them standard tunes, and -- you know, what you call music you're playing for the pictures is heavy stuff.
That's right, yeah. It's symphonic.
Yeah, like symphonic music.
Were there sessions around then,
after hours jam sessions, guys --
Not during that time.
Guys were jamming on the job.
Yeah.

You know, listening to these records, I've noticed not only on the Morton records, but on other records of this time, that instead of the whole rhythm section playing constantly throughout something, like we do now, that -- well, like Jelly would cut out -- well, there was an alto solo where there was just guitar, banjo, whatever he was playing at the time, and Jelly on the piano, and Baby Dodds. You didn't play on like 16 bars.
Uh-huh.

And then -- then everybody'd come back in, then there would be another section with maybe just drums and piano, and clarinet. To change the texture of the rhythm section. Was that a common thing back in the twenties?
I don't know, I never experienced that. Exception with Jelly. You know, on recording.
Yeah. Louie used to do that on some of his records, where the full band would play, and then come down to just Louie and --
New Orleans. New Orleans stuff.
That's New Orleans stuff?
Yeah, New Orleans stuff.
Yeah. Changed the texture of the rhythm section. And Jelly was the only one that you worked with that did that?
That did that, yeah.
That's interesting. Well, you said that when things got too rough musically, you'd go back to tuba to play the parts. Did you study string bass with anybody? Or how did --
Only my --
How did you develop as such a fine bass player?

Well, it was easier for me to learn string bass, on account of the violin. All I had to do was learn the fingering, the positions. Which is, you know, it's a little different. But it just seemed natural to me, just like the small violin. So it didn't take me long after -- oh, about two, three weeks, I could do pretty good on the string bass, you know, and I didn't have to change.
You just taught yourself?
Yeah.

You've always gotten a very beautiful dark sound on string bass. And I've noticed other bass players that have come out of Chicago have this dark tone. I'm now speaking of the sound of the tone. Did you strive for that, or do you feel that was just -- came out naturally
the way you played? William (Wellman) Braud was sponsoring me playing like I'm playing. Used to be with Duke. Duke's first bass player.
Right.

He's the one that taught me how to pick and hold -- told me I had to keep my fingers down tight on the fingerboard. You can't do like that -- when you put your fingers down on a string bass, you've got to put your fingers down and keep it down there while you're picking. To give the note the full value, you understand? Otherwise it would be just plucking like.
Right. Staccato.
Yeah. So he was responsible for that.
Well, how did you get together with Wellman Braud?

Well, when we played theaters. Sometimes like when I was at the Regal Theater with Dave Peyton, Duke Ellington's band played on the stage. They had a week there. And I got together with Braud. And then everytime he'd come into town, when I was at the Grand Terrace, he'd come by.
Did he teach you his slapping technique? Some of the records that he did with --
Yeah, well, I was doing that a long time before I met him. That's the only way I could get off
on string bass, because there was a lot of slapping going on back in them days.
Was that a novelty effect?
Yeah, that finally went out.
Except with Milt Hinton.
Yeah, he still slaps?
Oh, yeah, an awful lot. Takes solo, do a slap solo. Do a double slap. I was playing with him one time, I said, can you do a triple slap, and he did.
Yeah.

Well, to go back to bass players, after you became established, did you teach other bass players, or other bass players, younger bass players come to you, like Truck or Milt Hinton, and want you to show them something?
Well, I don't know when Milt Hinton started on bass, because he started on the bass shortly after -- seemed like me, after I did. Might have been in the thirties.
Yeah, I think he did.
See, because it was in the thirties when he left -- he went with Cab.
Right. Did you know Truck, Truck Parham?
Yeah. Well, you know, I met Truck. I can't remember exactly when I first met Truck.
Truck told me when he was a kid,
his family lived in Mecca Flats. And that he used to run beer for Freddie Keppard. Trumpet player.
Yeah, I've worked with Freddie.
You did? Where?
We worked out there, Villa Venice (PHONETIC).
Oh, Yeah?
Yeah. Guess who was in the band.
Who?

It was Shepperd -- what's his name, Freddie Keppard, Darnell Howard on saxophone, Bushell on saxophone, and who the heck was on trombone? Fellow by the name of Burt -- Burt something. Used to have a club at the Musicians Union. He played trombone. But the name I remember is Darnell Howard and Sidney Bechet, Freddie Keppard.
Bechet was in the band?
Yeah, Sidney Bechet. That's where I first worked with him.
Was that a fake band or a reading band?
It was a reading band. It was a road house.
Was Keppard a pretty good trumpet player?
Oh, my goodness yes. Fabulous.
What'd he play like? I mean, a lot of high stuff, or driving --
Lot of high, driving stuff. Real powerful. Boy, he'd blow you out of the room. He was -- well, he was big. Tall and big. He was a big man.
Yeah, I've seen pictures of him. I've also heard that he was sort of eccentric. A lot of the New Orleans musicians --
Yeah.
-- were sort of spoiled. People from New Orleans are strange, usually.

Yeah, there was a lot of things he didn't want to do, you know, because he didn't want nobody to see him play. Because he figured they'd take and steal his stuff. You heard that story about behind the net?
Yeah. And he was really like that?
Yeah.
Would he cover up his --

Yeah, I know he had a funny way of fingering, but, you know, I didn't know too much about valve stuff back in them days. Trumpets and things. But I knew the tuba. But I -- by me playing three valves, and him playing three valves, by the time (unintelligible) can't see what he's doing. But he'd be fingering like mad.
Was he as powerful as Louie Armstrong, or --
He's more powerful than Louie, yeah, he was more powerful than anybody I ever knew.
Yeah? Well, Bechet was pretty powerful, too.
Yeah, well he played soprano sax with us.
Yes, that's what I mean. Strong player. That must have been a pretty good band.
It was.
How long were you at the Villa Venice?
We weren't there too long. You know how them roadhouses go.
Yeah. That was a gangster joint, wasn't it?
Yeah.
Always has been -- or was, yeah. Who else did you play with back then?
I don't even remember what year that was. Must have been in between the time -- between Milwaukee engagements.
About the mid-twenties?
Yeah.
Were there other New Orleans musicians that you played with about that time?
Oh --
You mentioned Ory.
Yeah, Kid Ory, and what's the other trombone player from New Orleans?
Preston Jackson?
No. I worked with him, yeah, I worked with Preston. And this was back in the twenties.
Yeah, I know who you mean. I think I know who you mean.
Dutrey.
Yeah, Honore Dutrey.
Honore Dutrey.
Yeah. Was Natty Dominique up here then?
Yeah. I worked with Dominique.
Was most of the work in cabarets or nightclubs?
Yeah, most of it was cabarets.
How was the pay?
$35.00, $40.00 a week, which was big money back in them days.
Yeah. Were the tips good?
Yeah. Tips were real good.
What were the hours?
Six hours. Something like 10:30 to 4:30. Or 10:00 to 4:00.
Uh-huh. Did any of the bands rehearse, or did they just go --
Well, Tiny used to rehearse.
Tell me about Tiny Parham. He's sort of a mystery man to me. I don't know too much about him.
Yeah? Oh, yeah, he was a great musician. Heck of a piano player. He wrote all the tunes that we recorded; he wrote most of them.
Well, what kind of bands did he have?
Just about the same as Jelly's. Same instrumentation. Clarinet, trumpet, trombone, tuba.
Was he from New Orleans or Chicago?
You know, I don't know where Tiny was from. And you know that's Truck Parham's uncle.
It is?
Uh-huh.
I asked Truck about that one time and forgot what he said.
Well, that's what they tell me.
Well, was Tiny Parham pretty popular around Chicago?
Yeah.
Well, would the bands go from one club to another, or do they tend to settle in to one club, you know, like Reinhardt, or --
Yeah, they'd settle into one club. You didn't do too much jumping around, unless you got a notice or something, and then you started looking for another job.
Did all the clubs have shows?
Yeah. The smallest club had a show. Two, three girls, and two, three acts. Yeah.
Singers and dancers?
Singers and dancers.
And then the band just played for dancing?
Yeah.
And the show.
And the shows.
Did you get silly requests then, too?
Yeah.
What were some of the tunes that guys played back then?
You know, I can't remember. That's something -- that's been my problem, far as remembering tunes. Lot of times I'll play a tune and say, what the heck is the name of this tune? What am I playing now.
When did you start depending on your ear, as opposed to reading?
Well, that came natural. Even when I was taking violin lessons.
Really? That young?
Yeah.
You could play what you heard?
Play what I heard, yeah. Yeah, the minute you hit a note, I knew what it was.
You've got perfect pitch?
Uh-huh.
That's a great gift.
Yeah, we used to play games on the bus.
How do you mean?

One of the guys would ask me -- a train whistle would blow, or different sounds. What note was that Quinn? They called me Quee pee, that was my name, Que-pee. That was my nickname. What note was that, Que-pee?
Was this with the Earl Hines band?
Uh-huh. That's when we were traveling on the bus.
Train whistles always sound like a diminished chord to me.
Yeah. It's like a triad.
And that was --
Especially these diesel horns, you know.
Yeah. Sound like the beginning of "Dipper Mouth Blues,"
Yeah, (laughing).
When did you start arranging?

I started arranging when I was with Tate. I started arranging like Omer Simeon would arrange the saxaphone chords, I'd arrange the brass chords. They'd have what they called special courses. That's when I first started arranging.
What attracted you about tuba writing?
I didn't like to write. Then after I wrote a couple of brass chords and I heard it, I was fascinated with what I wrote. So when I went with Earl, I started making whole arrangements. The whole thing.
Did you ever study arranging or composing?
Yeah. With Louis Sanborn.
Oh, when --
When I was taking fiddle lessons in harmony and theory and arranging. I studied under him.
So you were getting that when you were 10, 11, 12, 13 years old?
Uh-huh.
That's really young. You recorded with -- to go back to Tiny Parham, you recorded with him. Do you remember when -- was that in the thirties, or --
Yeah, I think that was in -- let's see, now, that was -- had to be before -- couldn't have been the thirties, because it was before Earl Hines days.
Have to be the twenties, then.
Have to be the twenties.
Did Parham sing? Or do I have him mixed up with another piano player who sang?
I don't remember him singing.
When the Depression hit in '32, what were you doing, and how --
I was at the Grand Terrace then.
You were with Hines' band?
Uh-huh.
Did wages go down, or --
Well, don't even mention wages. During the Depression, because it all depended on what Ed Fox took in.
Oh, really?
Yeah. Things really got bad, you know. But I made it, you know. It was better than not working at all, you know.
Yeah. Did you ever have to take
After I left Earl I took a day gig.
When did Earl Hines first hear you?
Well, I guess it was when I was with Dave Peyton. At the Regal. He heard me play, and after Dave Peyton left, then Jerome Carrington took over the band.
Who?
Jerome Carrington.
Jerome Carrington?
Yeah, we used to play in the pit and on the stage. So at the time I went with Earl, there was five of us went with Earl at the same time.
Who were they?
Omer Simeon, Darnell Howard, Wallace Bishop on drums, Louis Taylor, trombone, and myself on bass.
Well, before we get into Earl, you say Peyton's band played in the pit and on the stage?
Yeah, on the stage it was under the direction of -- oh, I can't think of his name. He was an M.C.
Half Pint Jaxon?
No. You'd know him soon as I could think of the name. Oh, Fess Williams.
Oh, Fess Williams? Yeah.
Fess Williams, yeah.
Charlie Mingus's uncle.
Yeah.
Fess Williams. Interesting man. What'd you play on stage?
Oh, well, we had a show. You know, regular show.
You had a stage show?
Yeah. Chorus girls and everything. Acts.
Did the band do anything?
Yeah, we did band numbers. Did a couple band numbers. Called stage presentation.
What would the band do when they had a spot?
Oh, specialty numbers, you know. Special arrangements.
Were there-- guys take solos?
Yeah.
Like a jazz arrangement?
Just like a jazz arrangement, yeah.
How long were you at the Regal?
I was at the Regal about -- almost a year.
What is that --
I left the Regal in March, '31, went down to the Grand Terrace.
Well, you were telling me that's where Earl heard you?
I think so, yeah.
Did you know him before then?
I don't remember knowing Earl before that.
He was in Louis Armstrong-or Carroll Dickerson's band at the Sunset.
Yeah.
You ever hear that band out there?
You kidding? That's when I used to chin myself up to the window. I was in short pants then.
Did you know Louis?
Well, I worked with Louis at the Met. No, at the Vendome Theater.
Oh, really? Whose band was that?
That was Erskine Tate.
Erskine Tate's band? Was Louis--
He was a member of the band, and I filled in two weeks for the bass player. But Louis was a member of Erskine Tate's band, playing in the pit.
Did he take any solos?
Yeah.
Was he featured?
He was the -- featured, yeah.
Sing?
Yeah.
That was -- Armstrong, you know, just judging by the recordings from that time, was marvelous.
Oh, boy.
Were the guys really -- were they aware that he was as great as we know him today?
No, I don't think so. Not in them days.
He was just another one of the good players around?
He was just a good trumpet player, you know. He wasn't famous as he was -- as he got in later years, you know.
Was Jabbo Smith around town then?
Yeah. Jabbo used to come to the Sunset and challenge you.
Yeah? Who won?
The only man that I know that challenged Louie was Jabbo Smith.
Who won?
Hard to say. Because Jabbo was a tough man, too.
Yeah, very fast.
Yeah.
Very fast in those days. Did you play any with Jabbo?
Yeah, Jabbo worked with me up in Milwaukee in later years. Still . . . . the Wisconsin Roof Garden.
Wisconsin Roof Garden?
Yeah, that was with Floyd Campbell's band.
Right. When was that?
I don't know. Don't remember the year.
Before Earl?
That was after Earl.
After Earl.
Yeah.
Let's go to Earl now. But you hadn't known him before he offered you the gig?
No.
The band was pretty well established back -- this is 1931?
Yeah.
So the band was pretty well established then?
Yeah.
Yeah. And you took Hayes Alvis's place?
Hayes Alvis, yeah.
Was Hayes playing just string bass, or did he also double, too?
What was he playing? Yeah, I know he was playing tuba, I don't know if he was playing string bass then or not.
Well, you went in on string bass?
I went in on string bass and tuba.
Doubling.
Doubling.
I hate to skip around like this, but was doubling common in those days --
Yeah.
You played both, you didn't play just one?
You played both. You played both, you didn't play just one.
Did you have a preference, which you liked to play?

At that time I liked the tuba better than the string bass, because string bass was kind of rough for me back in them days, you know. It takes years and years to perfect -- to get the perfection on the string bass, and then
And you don't have that on tuba?
Not necessarily. It's not as technical as string bass. Because most of the time you're oom-pahing on the tuba. Unless you take a solo or something, you know.
Did you take solos back then?
What?
In the theater bands, or --
Yeah, jazz.
Did you have a feature?

Yeah, featured on me, yeah. Like that's where I first started playing "Asleep in the Deep," with Erskine Tate's orchestra at the Metropolitan Theater. I did it as a feature tuba solo, from beginning to end.
How'd it go over?
Great, beautiful, fact I played in church.
Really?
Uh-huh.
You played "Asleep in the Deep" in church, or --
I did a tuba solo in church, playing "Asleep in the Deep."
Did you have any other feature numbers that you did?
No, that's about the only, you know, name feature number I did, outside 'Tiger Rag.'
Uh-huh. You've been doing 'Tiger Rag' since then?
Yeah, for years.
Okay, now Earl. What was the band like when you'd go?
Well, I don't know. It was a good band, because -- you might as well say there was major changes he was making. He changed the five men, you know. Might as well say he was starting from scratch.
Do you know why he did that?
No, I don't.
Well, the first band had -- I know George Mitchell.
George Mitchell was with the first band.
Shirley Clay was in it, too?
Shirley Clay.
Were they still in the band when you joined?
Yeah..
Was the band's main job playing for dancing, or play the shows?
Main job was both.
Both?
Yeah. Played for the shows and played for dancing.
How big was the Grand Terrace?
I think it could seat about -- between three and four hundred people.
And it had a big dance floor?
Uh-huh.
What were the shows like back then? Were they bigger shows than --

Oh, my goodness, where you talk about elaborate, yeah, they were big shows. You'd have maybe about eight or ten just picture girls, then you'd have 16 chorus girls in the line. And at one time we had 12 chorus boys at the Grand Terrace.
And were there featured singers or featured dance teams?
Yeah. If you had -- like, you know, acts like you have today. Dancing acts and adagio acts, which you don't see much nowadays.
No. So how often did the shows change?
Every five weeks.
Every five weeks. Was that a six or seven night a week job, or --
Seven.
HEMLOCK
Seven nights? Was there a broadcast every night?
Uh-huh.
Every night?
Every night. Sometimes two, sometimes three times a night.
Did Earl ever say how he got into the Grand Terrace, or -- who was the guy who owned it, Ed Fox?
Ed Fox. Well, the gangsters owned it at first. Ed Fox was the manager.
When you say the gangsters, do you mean the remnants of the Capone mob?
The Syndicate, yeah, the Syndicate. The Syndicate. See, but when the government started cracking up on the books and things, then they just gave it -- they gave the joint to Ed Fox.
This was Capone's gang?
Yeah.
Did Capone used to come in there?
Once in a while. When I first started down there, then things got quiet. After they give up the joint --
(Inaudible).
Yeah. After they give up the joint to Ed Fox, then a few of the small, you know, echelons used to
come in. But it finally died out.
What was the band like? Who was in the band, do you recall some of the guys that you remember? In '31.
In '31? George Dixon, --
I saw George --
Darnell Howard --
-- at your night.
Yeah. He was there?
Yeah.
That's right, he was there. He was there with his wife. That's right. Him and Hilliard sat together.
You have George Dixon -- in the brass section we had George Dixon, Charlie Allen, Walter Fuller, and we had so many other trumpet players, man, I can't think of all of them.

Wait a minute, I'm trying -- I'm thinking about the band after we started broadcasting. After we got, you know, made all the changes. Got tight and everything, and started broadcasting. In the trombone section we had Louis Taylor and William Franklin. William Franklin sang and played trombone. In the saxophone section, as I say, we had Darnell Howard, Omer Simeon on lead sax, James Mundy on tenor sax, Cecil Irwin on tenor sax, and I think that was it

in the saxophone section.
George Dixon doubled trumpet and saxophone, baritone sax. So sometimes we had five saxes.
Yeah. That was rare for those days.
Yeah.
Very rare. Did you do a lot of rehearsing?
Yeah, we used to rehearse sometimes, a couple times a week.
Was Earl a good guy to work for?
Yeah.
Must have been.
Yeah, I never had any problems. Yeah.
Were you in the band the night that he got his nickname?
Yeah. Well, that was on the broadcast. Yeah. Because I was with the band before we started broadcasting.
When did the broadcasts start?
The broadcasts started in '32. I joined the band in '31, and the broadcasts started in '32.
I was looking in Earl Hines book last night, and just skimming through it I saw the story about the announcer --
Ted Pearson.
Yeah. Regular announcer.
Yeah, he's the one started calling him "Father" Hines.
Yeah. Fatha, Fatha.
Earl "Fatha" Hines. I don't know where he got that father from. Then after he'd make the announcement, then George Dixon's the one started hollering, "Father Hines, Father Hines."
Oh, he's the one that did that?
Yeah, he's the one did that.
That was a darn good band. You didn't work at the Grand Terrace all year round, did you?

No, after we started broadcasting, then, he started booking us out. We'd work sometimes about two or three months at the Terrace, and then go out two or three months and then come back in. In and out, in and out. Most of the time we'd leave after New Year's Eve. And go out and stay three, four months, and then come back in the spring.
You said "they would book." Would Fox book the bands?
Yeah. He didn't trust the different bookers, you know, like William Morris, and oh, different booking agents.
Well, when you went out --
It was easy to book the band then, because we was broadcasting every night.
Right. And you'd get nationally known.
Yeah.
Were they one nighters that you played, or did you have some --
The first time we went out it was a theater engagement.
Where was that?

I think that was at the Stanley Theater in Pittsburgh. And we played one night, I think. Then we came back to the Grand Terrace. Then the next time we went out -- theaters for three weeks. With a few one-nighters, you know, on the way there and on the way back. Then it started getting longer and longer.
More and more one-nighters?
More and more one-nighters. More theaters.
Were the one-nighters dances primarily?
Yeah, primarily dances.
What were some of the places that you went?
Well, Dreamland in New York, Savoy
Ballroom in New York. And the rest of the places I can't remember too well. Strand Ballroom in Philadelphia.
The Savoy, Chick Webb was the house band there?
Yeah.
You had cutting contests?

Right. We'd lose all the time. In fact, Duke Ellington even lost. Chick Webb, boy, he had a tough band, and tough arrangements. Oh, man. Boy, he had a whole band -- our bandstand would be jumping. And we wouldn't even be playing.
Were you opposite?
Yeah, opposite. One like over here, and we'd be at this end of the hall. Two bandstands.
How did those contests get started?
It became a commercial thing, I know, the Battle of the Bands.
Just automatically.
And who was the judge? The crowd?
The crowd, yeah. You know, naturally see, that was Chick Webb's home.
Yeah. Did Hines band play any other battles? With other bands?
No.
Just with Chick.
We'd play against other bands, but it
wasn't a battle. Like some places we'd play we'd have help, like when we played Tuskegee, Alabama, that's where I first met Hawk, "Tuxedo Junction" Hawk.
Erskine Hawkins?
Yeah, Erskine Hawkins. He was a school band.
Well, at the Grand Terrace, you did a lot of arrangements for -- you said that was the first you got into the full band arrangements.
Yeah.
What were some of the things you arranged?

I can't remember too many of them. A lot of the arranging we did was popular music. Back in them days they didn't have the guys, you know, to come around singing and going on, what'd they call them, tune pluggers. You didn't have them back in them days. So the different representatives from the publishing companies would come by Grand Terrace, and each one of them had their own arrangement -- own arranger. They'd pick out to do arranging on a new tune they got coming out. So I did a lot of those, Budd Johnson did a lot of them, Jimmy Mundy did a lot of them, and then --
Cecil Irwin did some arranging, too, didn't he?
Cecil Irwin did some arrangements before he got killed.
Did you get extra pay for that?
Yeah.
Did Hines pay you?
No, the publishing company paid you for that.
The publishing company?
Yeah.
Did they pay Earl to play it on the radio?
No. After we made the arrangement, we just goed ahead and played.
Did Earl have a straw boss at the Grand Terrace? I mean, somebody run the band, or did he, you know, call the tunes?
Oh, well -- no, he had a -- you wouldn't call him a straw boss. George Dixon used to conduct the band when Earl was off the stand.
But would Earl call the sets, or would George?
George called the sets. When Earl come on the stand, then he'd call the sets.
What were some of the interesting things that happened at the Grand Terrace in the early days,
that you might remember?
Well, I can't remember too much. Too many things happening.
Were the crowds varied? You said earlier that the pay depended on how the business was. So the crowds were up and down, would depend on what you --
Yeah, well that got along toward the last.
Uh-huh. What did the union say about that?
Wasn't nothing they could do. The union had to go along with them, too.
Is that why Earl finally left the Grand Terrace?

No. He broke up his band. While we was at the Terrace. He didn't leave on account of the money, he just left on account of he was intending to get like a cocktail lounge and play in it himself. That was his first idea of breaking up the band, and then after --
In Chicago?

In Chicago. Then after he got into the thing and it looked like it wasn't going to turn out so well, he decided to go back to the band. And he reorganized the band. But it wasn't the money -- wasn't the reason why he left the Grand Terrace.
Well, I guess he was one of the main reasons for the Grand Terrace's success.
Yeah.
If not the main reason. What kind of place was the Grand Terrace? I mean, was it ornate, or a lot of decorations?

Yeah, well, at first it was just like the old style cabaret, you know, a lot of drapes and things around there. And then they remodeled, and modernized the joint. So then it was did out in beautiful silver, new band-stand, everything. But it was a beautiful place.
Have a good piano?
Yeah, oh, they had, yeah. They had a German piano, don't hear of it much.
Bechstein?
Something like that. Becker's in it. Beck-something. Lord, it was long, about a block long. Baby grand. Wasn't a baby grand, block-long grand.
What do you think the reason is for the success of the Earl Hines band? In those days. The radio broadcasts, or --
Yeah, the radio.
Well, Hines himself was an outstanding instrumentalist. Did people really dig his playing, or --
Yeah, yeah.
I mean, they understood what he was doing?
Yeah.
Now, he sometimes can play -- still does, in fact, but back then play some pretty wild things.
Yeah.
Were they pretty much the same way all the time, or --
No, all together different. That's where my ear really came in handy.
Yeah?
Boy, it was a mess working with him, because he never played the something the same way.
Right, he played some funny --
Yeah, some funny chords.
Did you have any problem keeping up with him, or --
No, didn't have a bit of problem.
How'd the band get along with each other and with Earl?
Oh, fine. We got along fine.

Since that was a location job, some of the big bands, the leader sort of kept his distance from the other guys, you know. From what you've said, it doesn't seem to be the case with Earl. Was he -- well, when you were
Yeah, everybody traveled together. He traveled on the bus with us.
When did those accidents happen?

I'm trying to think when the first accident happened. I forgot the year. I think it was '35. We was in Iowa, traveling from Des Moines, Iowa to Minneapolis, open a theater engagement. You know, back in them days, a two-lane highway was real narrow. And one of those specially built trucks -- they had a flatbed truck and he had made it two-by-fours going across it like that, and sized that wide, to haul grain, you know, the farmers. And one of the corners of that body of that truck sideswiped just behind the bus driver. Just ripped that whole left side out. That's how Cecil Irwin got killed. Knocked him all the way back there, back with me.

The next accident was in '36. That was in the Cumberland Mountains. I don't know where we was going. We must have just left Baltimore, somewhere. Anyway, your road turned, and the bus driver didn't. He was after -- there was a loose bottle rolling up and down the aisle, and he turned around to tell somebody to pick up the bottle, and the road turned and he just kept going straight, and we went right down a 15-foot embankment. We landed at the bottom, end of the creek, and all

of that dust and running water, and reflection of the red lights from the bus on that dust, somebody hollared fire. And that did it. Me and Bish got hung up in the door upside down. The trumpet player, I don't know how the heck he got out, because you know, them buses had them windows that had the bars. I don't know how he got out, because when we got up to the top of the hill, up the road, he was standing up there waiting on us. I don't know how he got out of the bus. He got out that window some kind of way.
Was anybody hurt in that --

Yeah, Mitch-Bishop sprained his ankle. I think it was either sprained, or broke it. Anyway, he had trouble with it a long time. And a few minor injuries. The biggest one was when Franklin got his arm almost tore off and Cecil got killed.
That's still happening on the road, you know, the guys --
Oh, yeah.
It's always going to happen. Were you on your way to a gig when the accidents happened?
Uh-huh.
What -- you just cancelled the gig, or --
No, we played them. Show must go on.
Must have been tough, particularly
Without Cecil, yeah.
Had to go on and play after --
Uh-huh.
After Cecil'd been killed?
Yeah, then came home right after that. We filled out the engagements. Just what -- you know.
Must have been pretty rough traveling (inaudible).
Guess who sat in for Cecil in Minneapolis?
Lester Young ?
No, Prez .
Lester Young.
Lester Young. That's where I first met Lester Young.
(End of side 1.)
Just cancelled the gig, or --
No, we played them. Show must go on.
(Last several lines of side 1 repeated.)
That's where I first met Lester Young.
I'll be darned. I know he was up in Minneapolis about that time.
Yeah.
What'd you think of his playing?
Oh, man, he was murder then. Yeah, boy.
He always had that distinctive style.
Yeah, on the first records.
And he took Cecil's place?
Yeah.
How long did he --

I think we just filled out that engagement at the theater there. It was a split week. And I don't know whether it was the Friday, Saturday, Sunday, or whether it was Thursday. It was a split week. I know he finished out the engagement. Three days or four days. Then I think we came home after that.
It must have been pretty tough traveling in the South during the thirties?
Yeah, it was a little.
What do you mean?

Well, we never had any problems except that most towns we had to eat out of the A&P or something. Because you couldn't -- no restaurants you could eat in, unless you run into a town where they had one side for colored and one side for white. They had those kind of restaurants in the big towns.
Well, were you playing -- you know, in the South were you playing dances for black people, or were you playing dances --
White one night, and black the next.
In the same town?
In the same town.
How as the money on the road?
Well, couldn't say it was much. We didn't make but about $10.00 a night.
Really? When was that?

It was in the thirties. But that was during the Depression. You didn't have unions -- didn't have all that union tax to pay. Only tax we had to pay was like the -- the scales in the town we were playing in might be 50 cents or 60 cents.
Really?

That was all. You didn't have income tax, you didn't have nothing. That was all clear money. And that was enough money for me to send money home and still have money to live on. I don't know how the heck we'd do it. That was a heck of a ...
/(Inaudible).
Sure, I was raising these four girls.
At $10 a night.
Now you sit and you wonder, how could I do it. Like theaters only played $73.00. That was the scale.
Where were you living in Chicago?
Oh, on the Southside, between 59th and Michigan. I lived there for a long time. 58th and Michigan.
How long would the road trips be? How long would you usually be gone?
It varied. Sometimes two months, sometimes three months. The last one was nine months. That's when we went to California.
Was that your first trip to California?
Yeah. That was the longest.
How'd the band go over on the West Coast?
We went over everywhere we played. We went over great.
And, of course, you were recording a lot during that time, too?
Yeah, different -- like, you know, New York, we did most of our recording in Chicago and New York.
Did the band have any hits during that -- I know "Boogie Woogie on St. Louis Blues."
Yeah, that was one.
That was Jelly.
"Jelly, Jelly."
Did they have any in the mid-thirties?
I don't think so.
But they were on jukeboxes and --
Yeah, they was on jukeboxes.
I've always like that tune that you wrote when you were Earl.
"Blue Because of You"?
"Blue Because of You." By the way, Joe Johnson played that.
He played that, yeah. I heard it. I heard it.
Yeah, Murphy started his set with that.
Yeah, I heard it. What was I going to say? I forgot what I was going to say now.
Talking about "Blue Because of You".
Oh, yeah. I still get royalties on that.
Yeah. Did you write other things?
Yes, sir, it's selling. Do you know where it's selling?
Where?
Europe.
It's a beautiful tune. Beautiful tune. I'd like to get the sheet music on it, but I don't know where to get it.
I don't know where to find it.
Did you write other tunes?
I wrote "Harlem Lament".
"Harlem Lament"?
I just wrote that for recording purposes, and then I wrote "Dominick Swing".
"Dominick Swing"?
Uh-huh.
These were all with Earl?
Yeah.
Who's Dominick?

Your neck.

Oh, I see.

Uh-huh.

Henry Woods.
Henry Woods. And according to the story, it was rearranged by Cecil Irwin?
Uh-huh.
And then modified by you? Is that
It was?

"Rosetta".

Okay, so that's probably one of --

No, that was '34.
Still in the band.
I don't know what the heck kind of change I could have made on a Cecil Irwin arrangement. Unless I jazzed it up or something.
I don't know. Stanley Dance wrote that in the notes to the album.
Yeah?
And said that was the story. Didn't say it was true.
Didn't say it was true, said that was the story? You see, a lot of things you do, you don't think about it at the time. You don't know that it's going to go down in the history, or nothing.

Yeah.
Or '40. Somewhere in there.
Thirties. Must have been '39, because it's just before I left the band.

Last part, yeah. Last part of '40.
I see. But that '39, '40 band is an awful good band.
Yeah.
That was an excellent, excellent band. Really tight, and everything swung. Swung hard, too. You know, one of these records has an alternate take of "St. Louis Blues," but there's no yelling on it.
Uh-huh.

And it really -- you know, I'm waiting for it. I played it last night, and didn't realize I was playing the one that wasn't issued at the time. I said, 'I dolgarn know that there's some shouts on there.' George Dixon did those shouts?

He started that in the studio.
When he recorded it.

When we recorded it. And it sounded so good to him, Earl's solos, you know, He'd shout out different things. And when he said, 'Play it until 1951,' man, everybody started to figure, hey, are we going to be here that long? Oh, that was a long way off.
I guess that's easily the best known Earl Hines record.
Yeah.
And I think maybe the shouting had a lot to do with --
Had a lot to do with it. Had a lot to do with it.
I still hear guys do things like that, you know.
(Unintelligible) right now.
Right, right. Play it until 1991, or something.
Yeah, but I mean they do now.
Yeah, 1991.
That was probably George Dixon's greatest influence.
Yes.
(Laughter.)
The term has been used, supposedly by musicians in your days, picked up by writers, in describing the Hines' band as "Western swing." Did you ever hear that term?
Yeah. I heard that. I heard that.
When did you first hear that term?
I can't remember, but I remember hearing it.
Yeah. I guess, obviously --
It just started, it started in New York.
Sure. By New York musicians,
anything west of the Hudson is -- can't be very good, that attitude.
Yeah.
How do you see the difference between the Chicago musicians, you know, of the thirties, and New York musicians? The difference between the two -- two scenes?

It's very hard to say, because in the thirties, like when I was with Earl, like when we went to New York, I come to find out the majority of musicians, good musicians in New York were from Chicago. Was from the West.
That's right. That's right. But New York musicians I think still have a snobbish thing.

Yeah, you could always tell a New York musician, because like when we first went there, you had to go in and rehearse the show at the Apollo Theater, they had what they called -- the union had it, you had to have a stand-by band in the theater. Yeah, the competition is a little
stronger in --
They had a little problem the first time we went there, when we throwed those strings on them, for the show.
When was it that --
That was '31.
You went there that early?
Yeah.
And you played the Apollo then?
No, it was the Lafayette Theater.
Lafayette Theater.
Schiffman owned the Lafayette Theater, then the next time we went back it was the Harlem Opera House, owned by the same man, then the next time we went back it was the Apollo.
Were you at any sessions in New York?
No, I never made a session. I used to -- most of the time, Walter Fuller and I used to hang out at the 'Yeah Man.'
The Yowl Man?
The Yeah Man. That's where Billie Holiday was signing. She started out, her uncle was playing banjo and the guitar. Boy, and that chick used to -- boy, she used to kill us. We was there every night.
Your uncle was playing banjo --
No, her uncle.
Her uncle. Or her father? Her father was Clarence Holiday.
I don't know, could have been her father.
He played guitar and banjo with Fletcher Henderson.
Yeah. Well, it must have been her father, then. Boy, man, me and Walter Fuller was there every night.
You and Walter Fuller were pretty good friends?
Oh, yeah. Fact, me and Walter and George Dixon, well, quite naturally Louis Taylor and Wallace Bishop, we was all --
Same school.
Same school.
Did you visit each other's houses, and things like that?
Yeah.
Family type friendship?
Yeah, family-type thing. It was a surprisingly congenial band to be as large as it was, 16 pieces, you know, 16 men. No arguments, fights, nothing, the whole time I was with the band.
Any cliques?
No, except for what we called the Wet and the Dry.
Those who drank and those who didn't?
Yeah.
What was the larger group?
Hey, you know it was about half and half.
Really?
Uh-huh.
Was there much pot smoking?
That was the Dry half.
Oh, okay, now I get you. I thought you meant non-drinkers.
No.
I think maybe Chuck mentioned that division to me one time.
Yeah. Even with that division, we all got along fine.
The Wet and the Dry.
I used to get -- well, you know, I never did go for pot, but I used to like to get what we'd call a contact high.
Yeah. Well, that's still pretty much the way things are. Hasn't changed too much.
Yeah, same thing. Nothing changes.
Yeah.
As far as musicians is concerned.
Right, right. The social behavior, as we would say, of musicians is pretty much the same.
What was it like in Chicago in the thirties? You talked about how it was in the twenties. How was it in the thirties?
That was during the Depression, but --
There was a lot of music.
There was a lot of music going on.
Roy was down at the Three Deuces.
Roy was down at the Three Deuces. There was a lot of music going on. And Nance was downtown, you know, different places. Lot of bands out South. Wasn't making much money, but you were working.
Yeah, Albert Ammons had a good band out there.
Yeah.
How about sessions, were there many sessions around town? Places where guys would go after hours? Like you were saying in the twenties?
Yeah.
Jam a little?
Yeah.
What were some of those places?

Well, this first place I mentioned, at 55th and the el, that was around back in the thirties. That's when Art Tatum was here, and Teddy Wilson, just before Teddy Wilson went to New York. He was still around. Oh, my God, I don't know. Gang of musicians were around, and most everybody was working. You wasn't making much money, making $2.00, $3.00 a night, but you was working, and people was spending money. Especially, you know, the black population. We didn't suffer too much during the Depression, musicians didn't.
No, I know. Musicians seemed to do better then than later, really.
Yeah, cause I raised four daughters during the Depression.
Were there other big bands around Chicago then? That, you know, didn't get as well known as Earl, but good bands?
Big bands, I think we was the only big band in Chicago.

How do you see the basic difference between the Earl Hines Band in Chicago and the other big bands that were popular during that time? What was the special difference, besides, you know, the soloists?
The arrangements.
The arrangements?
Mostly the other bands had stock
arrangements.
Jimmy Mundy continued to write for the band after he left, didn't he?
Yeah, he did a little writing after he left.
Did the Hines Band use any stock arrangements, of, say --
Yeah --
(Inaudible).
Yeah, we used stocks.
Did you doctor them?
A few of them we'd doctor up. Not too many. We'd just play them like, you know -- most of the time we played stocks when Earl was off the stand.
Did Earl read well?
Yeah. Oh, yeah, he could read.
Did he play the shows?
Uh-huh. Played and conducted the shows.
(Recording interruption.)
Tell me something about when Earl broke up the band, had this falling out with Fox, and I've also heard that he had an offer to go with Benny Goodman, and, you know --
Oh, yeah.
What was all that?
I don't know. I don't know what happened with that, why he changed his mind.
Well, was he going to go with Benny?
Well, I don't know.
He was also talking about having his cocktail lounge.
This cocktail lounge, and, I don't know, that didn't seem to set well with him. He wouldn't have liked that no how, I don't think. Sitting in your own cocktail lounge playing piano.
Was he going to do a solo, or --
Yeah, he was going to sing -- oh, maybe a trio.
Well, whose idea was that? Was it his, or his old lady's, or --
Well, it was mostly his. With a few suggestions.
And that's all you care to say?
Yeah.
Well, he had this big thing with Ed Fox. The Union got into it, law suits, what do you recall of that time? I presume he'd already broken up the band?
Yeah. Well, I was with Fuller then.
Fuller took the band into the Grand Terrace?
Yeah.
How many of Hines' band went with Fuller?
Well, most of the band. See, we didn't have a bigger band -- he didn't have as big a band as Earl had. I think we only had about nine pieces on that band.
Well, did Earl feel this was being disloyal to him?
No.
Because he'd already broken up --
He'd already broken up the band. And as we saw it, looked like he was really going into this cocktail thing, at the time, so we just went on with Walter Fuller.
Because the gig was there?
Yeah.
You needed the gig. But as you said, business was getting bad then.
Yeah.
And what was the reason -- business had been so good, and then business fell off. Was it just that the crowd had gone some place else?
The crowd had gone, I guess, some place else. I don't know why.
You know, the usual thing, clubs
get hot --
People just -- yeah, and then people just stopped spending the money. Had to -- getting along towards the end of the Depression, you know.
Yeah, and there was more money.
Yeah.
Well, according to news accounts of the time, that gig didn't last too long, did it?
No.
They closed at the end of 1940?
Uh-huh.
And he owed the band $600.00, according to this Downbeat story.
Yeah.
Did you ever get the money from Fox?
No.
What ever happened to Fox?
I don't remember. I don't know what he did after that. I think he got out of the band business.
Was that the end of the Grand Terrace?
Yeah, as far as Ed Fox was concerned.
Well, did somebody else --
Somebody else took it over, after a while reopened it. It was a little different set up, though.
You mean physically, or didn't have shows, or --
You didn't have shows, yeah. No band. Mostly jukebox.
Oh, really?
Uh-huh.
So that was really the end of the Grand Terrace?
Uh-huh.
Had the gangsters pulled out?
Oh, they'd been gone a long time before that.
So the money was gone?
Uh-huh.
(Recording interruption.)
Well, did you stay with Fuller?
Yeah. We was out of a job for a while, then Fuller got this idea about the small combo.
Well, before we go into that, who was in the -- in Fuller's -- what'd you say, nine-piece band? Or eleven-piece band at the Grand Terrace?
Most of the Hines men. Omer Simeon who the stayed, I stayed/, Eck stayed on drums. I don't remember.
Was Oliver Coleman in the band then, or was that after Oliver?
I can't remember who the drummer was.
Well, who was in the small Fuller band?
Omer Simeon, Roselle Claxton on piano, Fuller on trumpet, and me on string bass.
Did you have drums?
Oh, yeah. Buddy Smith.
So it was a five-piece band?
Uh-huh.
Where'd you work?
Mostly cocktail lounges in and out of town. We worked the Capital, we worked in Peoria, Minneapolis, and you know, different cocktail lounges in and out of Chicago.
Fuller was a pretty good trumpet player.
Yes, he was.
Like Louie.
And singer, too.
And singer. Was he in -- it seems like I've seen where he's gotten credit -- partial credit for 'Rosetta.' Did he write the words?
He didn't write the words. He got credit for singing it. But I think Henry Woods wrote the music and the words, I think.
Were you glad to get off the
road? Or did you like traveling?
Well, I liked it when I went with Walter Fuller, because you stayed four weeks at the shortest.
Uh-huh. No one-nighters?

No one-nighters. Four weeks, with a two-week option, or four-week option. Sometimes you stayed eight weeks. Now, we was down in -- we stayed in Peoria, oh, about nine weeks. We stayed in Minneapolis at the Happy Hour about nine weeks, or more. No, we was there about -- well, it was nine weeks. ABout three or four months.
How long did that group stay together?
We stayed together, oh, almost two years.
I seem to remember coming up here -- I lived in Louisville, coming up here around 1944 and walking along Randolph Street, and seeing Walter Fuller's band.
Yeah, I wasn't with him then.
Yeah, but he still --
Still had a small band.
Yeah. When did he pass?
No, he's not dead.
He's not?
No, he went to California.
Lives in California?
Yeah, and he had a small combo for
years in San Diego. Then he got to be an officer in the union down there, and I don't know what he's doing now. I think he's still officer in the union down there.
I'll be darned. One of my favorite towns -- San Diego. I like the climate.
Uh-huh.
I didn't know that. That comes as a surprise. For some reason I thought that he had died.
No.
What happened after Fuller? With you?
With me? Well, there was still a small combo. After that -- oh, yeah,
(Inaudible).
After Fuller I went in the Rum Boogie, that's right. Because that was - what was that, '42?
Yeah, about '42.
Yeah, went in the Rum Boogie with Marl Young. And then went back in the Rum Boogie with Captain Walter Dyett.
Was the Rum Boogie sort of like the Grand Terrace?
Yeah, only smaller.
Now, the Grand Terrace had a big influence on South Side clubs?
Uh-huh.
Imitators.
Yeah.
What were some of the acts that you played in the parties? Recall any?
At the Rum Boogie?
Yeah.

Yeah, there was Barry Ruz (PHONETIC), and who the heck else was there? Oh, the dance act, called it The Lightning Flashes. I can't think -- oh, I can't think what the single acts were. There were still a lot of good acts in Chicago.
They were Chicago acts?
Yeah.
Well, were most of them --
(Recording interruption.)
Well, you did some recording with Jimmy Reed?
Yeah.

That's all we did.
Well, I mean besides with Jimmy?
Yeah, John Lee Hooker. And we did a lot of recordings, back-up, with the Spanials,, Jerry Butler. This was all when we was with VeeJay.
VeeJay?
Uh-huh.
Were you like the house bass player for Vee-Jay?
Yeah, like we was the house band.
Jimmy Reed's band?
Uh-huh.
Did you work --
No, Lefty Bates' Band.
Lefty Bates' Band?
Yeah.
And then Jimmy Reed would say, come in and --
Yeah, we was like the house band for We backed up all their artists.
Who else was in that house band? When was this, in the fifties?
Yeah.
Who else was in there?
It was different musicians from time to time, you know.
What was it, three or four man?

That was all the go then. They'd record his back beat. Then it'd all depend on how many men they needed for the session. He'd hire extra men.

Yeah.
He's an interesting man.
You telling me.
That reminds me of Mack, the guy that used to manage the Sutherland, back -- I keep thinking of McConnell but it's not McConnell.
Oh, yeah.
Know who I mean?
Yeah, I know who you're talking about. He was manager -- first was a bartender.
Yeah, and he said he used to work out at the Grand Terrace as a bartender.
Yes, he did.
Like -- Horace Silver wrote this "Filthy McNasty" tune for him. McLean.
McClean. We used to call him the Twiglet, that was his nickname.
The what?
Twiglet.
Twiglet?
Uh-huh.
Where did that name come from?
I don't know how he got that name, unless he used to wiggle behind the bar.
I haven't seen him for a long time. He's a nice guy.
Yeah, that's when we was at the Southerland. With Lefty Bates.
You worked the Southerland with Lefty Bates? Yeah. How long were you with Lefty Bates?
Eleven years.
Eleven years. And then you went into the --
Jazz, Limited.
What were some of the places you worked around town with Lefty?
The main place we worked with Lefty Bates was always -- jumped on Monday mornings, after -- at least the breakfast dance was the Trocadero
Where was that?
That was in the basement on 47th and Indiana.
I think I was at that -- that was one of those big old stone houses out there?
It was down in the basement of a hotel.
Well, I was at a place out there one time with John Steiner several years ago.
48th and South Park?
Somewhere around there.
In an old mansion-like house?
Mansion-like thing. Big stone --
Yeah. Also worked there.

And this lady owned the building, and she used to have an after-hours place down in her basement, which she still has. Doesn't run it any more. And she had pictures of Louie, and Earl, and all these -- Sid Catlett, all these guys that had been there. Yeah, you worked at that place, too?
Yeah, I worked there, too, with Lefty.
Are there places like that any more?
I think there's one at 48th and Indiana, down in the basement, that's still going. Blues joint.
Did you find -- well, these V-eJay recordings, --
(Recording interruption.)
Did you find it much of a switch going from, you know, a big band like Earl, and then Walt Fuller's band, and then playing with guys like Jimmy Reed you know, or blues like that?
No, it wasn't hard. Because, you know,
Sometimes 12 and a half, 12 and a quarter.
I just used my ear. That's when my ear come in handy.
Yeah. Came in handy, again. But when you went out and worked clubs with Lefty, was that mostly blues, or rhythm and blues?
Rhythm and blues.
Lot of singing, and things like that?
Yeah.
Did you do some singing?
No, I didn't do any singing. Lefty did some singing. And we had a piano player that had a voice like Billy Eckstine.
Speaking of Billy Eckstine, were you in the band when Billy came in?

Yeah, I was in the band when we picked him up. Yeah, he wasn't even playing trumpet then, yet. He learned the trumpet on the road while we were playing theaters He would practice in the dressing room on his horn.
Well, he's known for 'Jelly, Jelly,' and was it 'Water Boy,' was another one he made?
Uh-huh.
What kind of guy was he then? Must have been pretty young.
He was -- oh, yes, he was real young.
Was that his first --
I imagine the first big time, out of the Crystal Caverns in Washington.
How long was he with the band?
He was with the band until the band broke up.
In forty?
In forty. Then when the band was reorganized, he went back with the band.
Right. And that's when he made "Jelly, Jelly", wasn't it? And "Stormy Monday," or were you on those records?
Yeah -- huh?
Were you on those records?
I don't think I was on those records.
Maybe Chuck was on them.
Chuck was probably on them.
Was he doing blues when he first came with the band, or was he more a pop singer?
Well, he turned everything, blues and pop.
Did he have --
He was an all-around singer.
Did he have that pronounced vibrato then?
Yeah. Ballads and all that.
And he was pretty much as we know him now?
Yeah.
You know, the sound.
Yeah.
Well, were you in the band when Sarah Vaughan came in?
No, I left -- I'd already left the band.
And Dizzy and Charlie Parker?
Yeah.
That was afterwards?
That was afterwards.
Was Earl much of a disciplinarian?
No.
Did he leave that up to George?
He left it up to -- I imagine he -- I would say he left it up to the band. We policed our own selves.
He was pretty easy going?
Yeah. Mostly everybody in the band was strictly business, you know. Never late, always on time,
on the job. No heavy drinking, no drunkards.
Did you have a fine system?
Yeah, but we didn't need it.
Did the guys practice a lot, keep up on their --
Well, we used to -- the band used to rehearse about -- maybe once a week. Sometimes twice a week.
Before the job, or in the afternoon, or --
Afternoon. Sometimes we rehearsed when we got off.
Yeah, bands used to do that. Then you'd have to rehearse all these new arrangements?
New arrangements.
And you said the show changed every --
The show changed every five weeks.
So you had a whole bunch of music.

We'd have a whole bunch of music. Now at the show -- rehearse with a piano player until the day before the show was to go in. Maybe might rehearse two days before the show. Then we'd have a dress rehearsal the same morning, when we'd get off, if the show was to open that night.
Now, these were not only different acts, but different routines for the chorus girls and --
Yeah, yeah.
But the chorus girls remained the same?
Yeah.
So there was a lot of music to rehearse?
Lot of music to rehearse.
Who produced those shows? Venable?
Percy Venable, Valaida Snow, and Andy Razaf and another song writer produced a couple shows, hailed from New York.
Did Charlie Carpenter have a hand in that?
No.
He takes a lot of credit for things in Earl's book. Was he that important?
Maybe after I left. But he was -- the only thing he did while I was with the band was take care of Earl's correspondence. And things like that. Take care of the different businesses.
Well, judging from the book, he was pretty much the reason for Earl's success, from what he says?
Well, he made a lot of suggestions. He was a real show mind. He made a lot of suggestions. He
was really show-minded.
He was quite young, too.
Yes, he was.
Right out of high school?

No, we didn't start wearing tuxes until we moved in the new place.
When was that?
Moved there sometime around 1960. I can't remember exactly when, because I hadn't been with the band too long.
Yeah, you were in the new place when I came to town, which was 1960's, so -- who were some of the other musicians that went through the band? In all those years you were there?
Art Hodes Miff, some other big name jazz musicians. Jack Teagarden, Mole --
They'd come down and sit in, or --

I mean when you were in?
No, that was before my time.
But I mean when you were in it, who were some of the musicians that came through?
Well, that was about it.
Didn't Nappy play a while?
Yeah, Nappy filled in, you know, on trumpet, when we needed a trumpet player. Filled in.
Well, Bobby Ballard came into the band.

When did Barnett come in?

Went back to New Orleans.
