Yes, he is. Great drummer.
Yeah, he and you got along very well.
Got along fine.
Well, you were playing tuba and string bass? Weren't you?
Uh-huh.
And you were featured on 'Tiger Rag' and 'Asleep in the Deep'?
'Tiger Rag' and 'Asleep in the Deep.'
On tuba.
On tuba.
Did you have any preference of which instrument you played with Reinhart?
With Reinhart the tuba went better than the string bass, on account of the New Orleans tempos.
Or the attempts at New Orleans tempos.
Slow, lazy, two-beat things. Tuba went better.
How long were you at Jazz Limited?
12 years.
Until they closed?
Uh-huh.
Did that band play very much on the road?
No, very seldom. Every now and then we might make a trip, little short trip like up to Michigan, or something, you know, on the holiday for one night. Right back to Chicago.
And I know it made one album on Atlantic, Reinhart's band, that you were on.
Uh-huh.
Were there any others?
No, that's the only one I made.
Just that one?
Yeah.
(End of side one.)
Let's talk about arranging a bit. Did you do much arranging after you left Earl?
No, I didn't.
You just sort of wrote whatever band you were in -- you --
Yeah. Well, after I left Earl, got me working with small bands, there wasn't much need of an arranger.
Well, did bands other than those that you were working with, did they ever sound you about arrangements?
No.
You just wrote for whoever you were working with?
Yeah.

Who influenced you in arranging, if anybody? There are so many things -- like I was talking last week about the sax solely on one of the tunes that you arranged. It sounds very much like Fletcher Henderson. Did you listen to other arrangers, and say, gee, I'd like to do something like that? Say a Fletcher Henderson arrangement?
Yeah, that's right. Fletcher Henderson, and Duke, and a lot of the big bands.
Who was your favorite arranger?
Duke Ellington, quite naturally.
Yeah, because of the voicings and --
Because of the voicing he had. I tried to get that voicing, but that's kind of hard to do.
I was driving home this morning from the gig, and Dick Buckley was playing broadcasts from
1940 of the Ellington band. My, my, my, what a band that was.
Yeah.
Did you hear that band very much?
Yeah, I heard them a lot.
Yeah? Did you hear Blanton a lot?
Uh-huh.
What was your impression of him?
Very outstanding bass player. Phenomenol. The technique he had on the string bass was something else.
Yeah. Duke featured him a lot, too.
Uh-huh.
Well, did that sort of change your way of thinking about string bass?

Well, not exactly. Other than tried to get some solos together myself, you know what I mean. Listen to him, and watching his fingering, and everything, well, being an ex-violin player, it came easy to me, you know. All I had to do was just get my ideas together.
Uh-huh. Did you do much bowing work?
Yeah, I did a lot of bowing work with Lefty Bates.
Really? That surprised me a little, because from what you've said earlier, it was sort of like a
rhythm and blues entertaining group.
Well, it was, but I had some solos I used to take on string bass, and I'd bow them instead of picking.
Oh, I see. Like Slam Stuart?
Like Slam, yeah.
Would you sing with it?
No.
Just arco
Just arco.
Who was most helpful to you in string bass?
Well, starting out I'd say Wellman Braud, , Duke's bass player with his first band.
Uh-huh. You'd said something about he taught you to --
Taught me how to keep my fingers on the keyboard, on the strings, when I'm picking, in order to get that full tone.
Who after Wellman Braud?
That was really about it.
Do you feel that you're --
Unless I could pick up by ear, you know, like I'd say Jimmy Blanton, Ray Brown, just by listen- int to different bass players.
What about tuba? That fellow's name that I was trying to think of last week who had recorded with Louie Armstrong was Pete Briggs.
Yeah, yeah, I know Pete Briggs. I knew him real well.
Tell me something about him?
He was a great tuba player. Really had good ideas on bass solos. I mean, he could really get over that tuba. Yeah, I remember him real well.
He was around Chicago in the late twenties, wasn't he?
Yeah.
Did he have an influence on you, you know, like you were talking about Wellman Braud, you know, being of great help to you. Was there anybody in that regard on tuba?
Yeah there was several tuba players around here then back in those days, played tuba solos, that had influence on me.
Who were they?
Well, Pete Briggs is one, that other name I recalled the other week --
Beauford.
Beauford.
Is that Beauford Collins?
His last name, I think, was Beauford. He made some records with Jelly, too, after I did.
Yes.
He was one, and then another tuba player, Mays.
Mays?
Yeah, I can't think what his first name.
Who'd he play with?
Oh, he gigged around here. All those were old-timers. Then when I started, everybody was gigging and going on. That was back in the twenties. Some of them had regular jobs, and some of them didn't.
Well, did they play -- what's the difference between a tuba and a sousaphone? Is there any?
There's no difference, both of them are tubas. I look at the sousaphone like the baby grand of the tubas.
It's larger?
Yeah, it's larger.
And that's what you played?
Uh-huh.
You'd get a better tone out of it?
Better tone.
Depth?
Better tone, depth, and everything.
Does it execute faster?
Not necessarily. About the same.

How do you get your chops together on tuba? You said you hadn't played for about 30 years, and your chops hadn't gone away. But it seems like such a difficult instrument to play, filling all that with -- all that tubing with wind.

Yes. Oh, I don't know, I just had -- might as well say I just had strong chops. Many a time I was in that military band I was in, that 1924 band, a lot of times we'd go on marching jobs, and I'd be the only tuba in the band.
Oh, yeah?
25, 30 pieces.
That takes a lot of stamina, and stuff like that.
Yeah, I know. It just came natural to me. I didn't have a bit of problem, just blew.
You had a little thing that you used to do with your hand at Jazz Limited, when you soloed.
When I applaud when I get through a solo?
Yeah, unbelievable.
This left hand?
Yeah.
Some fellow was here with a convention one time, and I think he was from New Orleans, or somewhere down South. Anyway, he gave me a left hand glove. It was illuminated, to use for that.
Really?
Uh-huh.
Did you do it?
Yeah, I used it. He said he brought it especially for "Tiger Rag."

Who were some of the musicians who really knocked you out? Your career goes back to the twenties, and you were really, you know, sort of right in the development of this whole music. A lot of great musicians.
In the twenties I'd pick Sidney Bechet and Freddie Keppard, trumpet. And Johnny Hodges, saxophone, Art Carney on baritone sax --
Harry Carney.
I mean Harry Carney. And Lawrence Brown, trombone. Quite naturally, Duke. Lester Young. That knocked me out, playing with Les.
Yeah. That was '34, I think you said?
Yeah, '34, the year we played -- we had the accident and played --
In Minneapolis.
At the Orpheum in Minneapolis. Oscar Pettiford on bass, when I was up in Minneapolis.
He was a young fellow then.
Oh, yeah, he was real young, then.
His family had a band, right?
His family, whole family --
Sisters were playing.
Sisters.
Did you hear that band?
Yeah, I heard it. Heard it in Minneapolis.
Was it a big band or small band?
Small band.
And that's where you first heard Oscar?
That's where I first heard Oscar.
What was he playing like then?

Well, he was playing a lot of solos, and technical solos, and getting over that bass like it was a small violin. You know, between him and Jimmy Blanton, they really fascinated me when it come to playing bass. I couldn't -- you know, I thought it was phenomenal, because that's the first time I heard bass players, you know, taking jazz solos and playing them like that, on the string bass.
The position is a left-hand -- the problem is --
Yeah, fingering. Yeah.
Who were some other musicians that impressed you?
Well, Darnell Howard, Omer Simeon, saxophone.
Was Simeon on saxophone rather than clarinet?
Both. Yeah, he was a terror on both. Beautiful first sax.
Yeah, beautiful sound.
And he never got credit.

No, he didn't, because -- I think it's because these records that he made with Jelly Roll became, you know, such classics, and he played such beautiful clarinet on them that, you know, a lot of people think that you can do one thing, then you can't possibly do something else.
Can't do something else.
But his work with Hines on albums.
On alto, just beautiful.
I saw him with Jimmy Lunceford's band in the mid-forties. He was playing lead alto, I think. He didn't play much clarinet. That's the only time I ever
saw him. Yeah, he was a great saxophonist, but also a clarinetist.
Trying to think of some of the other great musicians.
Did you hear Roy much down at the Three Deuces?
Roy Eldridge?
Yeah?
I used to go (down there all the time.
Was he one that you say impressed you?
Yeah, Roy Eldridge, Red Allen. Oh, boy. Quite naturally, Pops-- Louie Armstrong.
When did you first hear Dizzy? Did you hear him when he was with Earl's band, you know, after you had left?
I think I first heard Dizzy, seems to me, with Fletcher Henderson.
Fletcher or Cab Calloway?
I know it was in New York.
But he worked with Cab for a while. I guess that was before he worked with Hines. He was with Hines around '42, something like that?
Yeah, I think so.
He'd also worked with -- saxophone player that had the big band that Roy had played with for a while in New York. Teddy Hill.
Oh, Teddy Hill?
Yeah, he was with Teddy's band for a while.
Yeah, that's right. I remember.

When Dizzy and Charlie Parker got together and it was supposedly a new kind of jazz came together, did you find that threatening or surprising, like some of the musicians who'd been playing a while did?
No, I didn't. In fact, I liked it. Yeah, I enjoyed that style.
You seem to have always admired guys with good chops.
Good chops, yeah.
And the harmonic aspect of that music, too.
Oh, yeah.
Ninths and flat fives, which -- well, those things had gone on before, hadn't they? I mean, they didn't invent the flat five or the automatic 13's.
No, they didn't invent them, but it was the first time I heard them play Bach melody. That's what's fascinating to me.
That fast moving line?
Yeah, that fast moving line. They had a lot of imitators, but it didn't sound as good as they did.

I heard, for the first time last night, on the broadcast also, the band that Dizzy took out to Billy Berg's in 1945 or '46. Forty-five, I think it was. Charlie Parker, and Milt Jackson was in the band. And this was a broadcast. And, oh, gee, it was really -- it really was mind-blowing to hear that band after all these years, because I've talked to Dizzy a lot about it and Ray Brown and Milt Jackson, but it never recorded. And then to finally hear it as I'm driving, and it's a broadcast, it really was a trip.
Yeah, I know.
Who were some of the other musicians, after these guys? You mentioned Cannon, and --
I don't know. I think that's about it. I can't think of nobody else, right off hand.
And in arrangers, you talked about Fletcher Henderson, and Duke.
....Duke . Jimmy Mundy . Budd Johnson.
Do you have any of your scores?
Sy Oliver.
Sy Oliver, right. That's another one. Did you have any of your scores?
I haven't got a one of my scores.
Whatever happened to those arrangements?
I lost them in moving, I guess.
Well, did you, after Earl's band broke up, did you get your parts back, or did you just have the score, or --
No he kept -- I just had the scores.
So he kept them?
I kept the scores.
But he kept the parts?
Yeah, he kept the arrangements.
I wonder whatever happened to that book. I understand just a few things remain.
I'd like to know. I'd like to know what he did with that book.
When he used to come to town, I remember I was working with Truck some place. And a lot of the guys who had been through the band would have a party for Earl, sort of like a reunion.
Yeah.
What were those like? And, you know, who put them together? Was there sort of like a club of ex-Earl --
Yeah, that was mostly done by guys
like George Dixon and Willie Randall, (P- U-)
And everybody would get together when Earl came to town?
Yeah.
What would you do?
Just sit around and talk and drink. Talk about old times.
Yeah. Do any playing at those sessions?
No.
Just talked?
Just talked.
There's a lot of the ex-Hines band still around town. Have you all stayed in touch, much.
Very seldom. George and I keep in touch with each other every now and then, through a mutual acquaintance. Works the same place George works, downtown at the police headquarters.
George works for the police?
Yeah, elevator starter.
After Jazz Limited closed, where were you working next?
Well, I was mostly jobbing, and like I worked Jazz Five. at
That's right.
And the In Place on Sundays.
With Jerry?
With Jerry Fuller.
That's right.
I did that until I got sick and went in the hospital.
When was that?
Must have been somewhere around '73, I guess, or '74.
Yeah, I remember when you first went in.
Jazz Limited closed in what, '72?
Yeah.

And I did a lot of gigging, with Art Hodes, Bill Tinkley. And I did that until the very fine president of the Gas Light Band would hire me on Sundays. He was working at Alfred's. That's when I started with Joe Kelly.
Johnny Board's in that band now. Was he --
He was in the band, yeah.
Who was in it? Barrett Deems on drums?
Yeah, and Larry on saxophone, from Czechoslovakia. And Joe Kelly, he was a real -- Michael
Fuller on piano. That was the band when I started.
When did you go into the Gaslight Club?

I went into the Gaslight Club shortly after that. I went in there to make an album with Joe Kelly. And then he finally persuaded Mr. Brown, Burton Brown, to put the bass on. So that's when I started at the Gaslight.
When was that?
This is '77, and I was there five years --
'72. Yeah, that was '72 when I started with him. At the Gaslight.
When did John Board come in?
John Board came in, I think, about two, three years, now.
He's a good tenor man.
He's a good tenor man.
I think I first heard him when he was with Hampton, a long time ago.

And after the -- we left the Gaslight and we worked a lot of jobs around town, like the Raw Onion. And Big John's Distillery, and Captain's House, and The Hanger, out in -- out west here in town, out west here, right at the toll road. Can't think of the name of the town --
suburb.
Addison?
No, it wasn't Addison.
Well, then you went back into the Gaslight?
Then we went back into the Gaslight. After we went back in the Gaslight that time, we stayed there.
What does that band play, mostly, at the Gaslight?
Well, what we call Chicago jazz. Wasn't Dixieland.
More swing?
More swing, like the Chicago, Chicago jazz.
Hard driving?
Hard driving.
Mostly four-beat?
Yeah, mostly four-beat. More than two.
When did Barrett leave?
Barrett left -- when we left the Gaslight, Barrett stayed in the Gaslight.
Oh, that's right, he'd been hired separately.
He was hired separate. He stayed in the Gaslight when we left.
I remember it. And he started using Johnny Board, I recall while, ...to get it correct in my mind. I know he told me about it. He had a trio, I think. Maybe quartet.
I can't remember exactly.
Different people were there, I think. The trombone player was --
Yeah, because Barrett stayed with all the different bands that was there.
Complaining all the way.
Yeah.
Of all the bands you played with, what was your favorite?

Well, my real favorite band, big band, was the Earl Fatha Hines. And my little band was Lefty Bates band, until I joined Joe Kelly. And after John Board started with Joe Kelly, then we really got together on, you know, different arrangements, and suggestions from Johnny Board. He really brought the band out. He would swing, all together different sound. We sounded like a 16-piece band.
Yeah, I know. He's got a good sound. You liked the more arranged groups, rather than the loose --
Yeah. Even if they were head arrangements, I liked it.
Did you get involved in a little arranging again at that time?
No, I never arranged any more music, after Earl, that I can remember. After I switched to the little bands, then I stopped arranging.
So you like the Lefty Bates' group, and Joe's?
Yeah, and Joe Kelly. Them two were the greatest sounding little bands I ever worked with.
Things were worked out in both groups?
Yes.
Well, Lefty's band, was that piano, bass, and guitar, or drums?

When we first started, we started out with a trio, piano, bass, and guitar. Then we added drums. Then we added saxophone. And let me see, what did we add? Saxophone; we already had the rhythm section, with the bass, guitar, and drums. Then we added that saxophone.
Who was playing saxophone?
Oh, we had a lot of different saxophone players. Boy that was with Duke for a while.
In St. Louis?
No, he's from Chicago.
Alto player?
No, played tenor.
Tenor?
And had --
(Recording interruption.)
-- Cliff Davis on sax at one time. (Inaudible).
Is that Eddie Johnson, the tenor man?
No, Eddie Johnson never worked with us. I worked with Eddie Johnson with the -- Merle Young's band at the Rum Boogie, during the war.
Is there anything that you've regretted over the course of your career?
No, surprisingly enough. No, not begrudge it. All these years of playing music, I still don't regret my move I made back in 19 -- when was that, 19--
1926, wasn't it?
1926. When I left school and went out to Milwaukee to play. Haven't regretted a minute of it.
I don't think you should. Was there anything, during all those years, that really stands out in your mind, being out of the ordinary?
Beyond the ordinary? I can't think of anything now.
(Recording interruption.)
You recorded with Benny?
I recorded with Benny, yeah, when he was here. I remember how bad he was. He was kind of funny. His brother was playing bass fiddle with him then.
Yeah, who was that?
His name was Goodman, too. (Harry)

Let's see, the trumpet player, he (Goodman) was Irving. / Yeah, and then the other brother was playing bass. In fact, Teddy Wilson told me that's why the trio was a trio, and not a quartet. Because they really didn't make it on bass.

Yeah, the bass player. So Lionel knew about me as he was raised here in Chicago. So he recognized me as being good, and I made that session one time, for old Victor. On Lakeshore Drive, right there at the S-curve.
Yeah, by the Drake Hotel?
No, it was on the outer drive, just before you go into that big grey building over on the east side of the Drive, just before you get to the S-curve?
Oh, yeah.
Going south? That's where Victor used to be.
I see. Well, about when was that?
It must have been around 1939, later, after I'd left Earl. Must have been in the forties.
Well, was Hamp still with Goodman then?
Yeah. Hamp was still with him, and let's see, Ziggy Elman (PHONETIC) was with him, Harry James, and -- I'm trying to think of the tenor players. That was the old Benny Goodman band.
Bud Freeman was with him for a while.
Yeah, Bud Freeman.
Arthur Rollini, I believe, was with him.
Yeah.
That must have been earlier than 1940, because a lot of those guys had left about '38, '39, somewhere in there.
Well, I know this was -- I hadn't been working. And I wasn't with Earl then, I don't think.
Well, do you remember what you recorded with Benny?
No, I can't. I'm trying to think of the name of that tune we recorded with Ziggy Elman.
Under Ziggy's name?
No, under Benny's name. He did the feature trumpet, like that Jewish thing he did.
Oh, yeah, like in 'The Angels Sing.'
It wasn't 'The Angels Sing,' it was another one he did.
Have you gotten credit for this in
I don't know. I don't think so.
I don't think so, either.
I don't think so, either. I'm not listed in any of that stuff.
But you did do this --
Yeah, I did do that. I remember doing that session, one session.
About how many tunes were recorded, do you remember?
Oh, about four tunes.
Four tunes. That's a pretty standard --
Yeah, that was pretty standard back then.
Gee, it would be nice to know at least one of the titles.
Just like I say, when I was recording, I never paid too much attention to titles. A lot of that stuff I never figured would be history, you know.
(Recording interruption.)
Interviewer's insert: The session that Quinn talks about, Benny Goodman session, research, it was May 4th, 1939. It was Goodman's last Victor recording session before he went with Columbia.

The tune that he mentions that Ziggy Elman played on, or was featured on, was "Who Will Buy My Bublikhki". The other two tunes on the session were, the big band version of "Pick a Rib," and "You and Your Love," which had a vocal by Martha Tilton.

Russ Connors' Biodiscography of Goodman does not have this information, except that it mentions that it's possible that Quinn Wilson was the bass player. So Quinn has confirmed that he was the bass player. This information has been sent to Russ Connors for whatever purposes he cares to make of it.
Back to the original interview.
Just like I say, when I was recording, I never paid too much attention to the titles, because a lot of that stuff I never figured would be history, you know.
Yeah. Well, of course.
Like I forgot a lot of them tunes I made with Jelly, because I was just on a recording date.
Yeah.
Now looking back, 50 years later --
Just another gig, huh?
Yeah.
Well, did you know what to expect when you recorded with Jelly? Had you heard any of his records, or you just --
No, I hadn't heard any of his records. In fact, I didn't know him. Until I got there, went to the session that day.
That was done for Victor, too.
Uh-huh.
It was a different place, though, back then?
That was a different place.
That's the one, I think that was, near the Drake Hotel.
Yeah, just across the street on Michigan Avenue, Michigan and Oak?
Somewhere like that.
Somewhere like that.
But you didn't know what to expect?
NO.
Was it a morning session, or afternoon session, basically?
Afternoon.
Did you know any of the other guys on the date?
Yeah, well, I knew Omer Simeon. And Shirley Clay, trumpet player. And I didn't know Mitchell real well, but, you know, I knew him casually.
George Mitchell?
George Mitchell.
But Johnny and Baby Dodds were on --
They were on some of those sessions, too.
Did you know them before that session?
No, I'd heard them, but I didn't know them. That's the first time working with them.
Well, you say you didn't know Jelly before then. Had you heard anything by him?
No, I hadn't even heard anything by him.
Did you have any contact with him after the sessions?
I don't remember. I don't think so. Because I think he left town after that.
Yeah, I guess he did, a year or so after that, then he went to New York. Do you remember the diamond tooth in his --
Yeah, I remember the diamond tooth.
Well, this Goodman session is fascinating. And you say Ziggy Elman did one of those frillica (PHONETIC) --

Yeah, I remember that. Oh (unintelligible) I think there was Martha Tilton, and I think she did the vocal. I think she was on that session. One of those vocalists was on the session. I think it was Martha Tilton.
Yeah, I think she was with the band at that time. Did she sing on the Ziggy Elman thing?
No.
That was all Ziggy?
That was all instrumental.
And you say you think there were four songs. They were issued?
Yeah.
Well, that will give the researchers something to dig for.
Yeah, find out what happened. Because I was the bass player of record on there, because he didn't use his brother.
Yeah. Was Gene Krupa still in the band, or was Dave Tough playing, or --
No, Dave Tough wasn't playing. Gene Kruppa was in the band.
Gene was still in the band.
Yeah, he was still in.
Tell me something about Lionel. You told me something about when he was a kid, used to play on the curb, and so forth.
Yeah, we used to go down on the curb, stand around the picket fences and sidewalk. Still humming like he does now. He was humming then.
Yeah, one of the great jazz grunters.
Yeah.
Well, did you re-establish contact with him in the thirties? Well, obviously if you --
I lost contact. The only thing, I just heard about him being out on the Coast, and the different bands he was in. Then I heard right when he organized his old band.
Yeah, but before then, was this Goodman session, and you said that he got you on this session.
He got me on that session, yeah. He was traveling with Benny then.
So he still remembered you and --
Yeah, he still remembered me.
Was he at the session?
Yeah, he played on the session.
Drums or vibes?
Vibes.
Well, he recorded your tune, also.
Yeah, 'Blue Because of You.'
Yeah. Did he let you know he was going to do that?
No, I didn't learn about it until I heard it on 's session one night. I was coming home from the Gaslight.
And that's the first you knew about it?
That's the first I knew about it.
Well, he recorded it in like 1939.
Yeah.
And then you're talking about the seventies, and you didn't know?
I didn't know nothing about it.
I'll be damned. Seems like somebody would have mentioned that to you.

Only ones they mentioned -- I knew about Earl, we recorded it about two or three different times. Only others I remember was Fats Waller made it. And who else, somebody else made it. I forgot who it was now. I was surprised.
Yeah, Hamp's record is nice.
Do you remember who was on that record with him?
I don't remember. All I remember, you know, is Hamp's playing on it. I'd have to look it up. And that's the only time you've ever heard it?
Uh-huh.
Let me see what I can do about getting you a copy of it. Yeah, that-- in fact, that's the first time I heard the tune, was Hamp's record. I hadn't
heard Earl's record of it. But I was familiar with Hamp's record of it. And I didn't know that you two had this long --
Yeah, we raised up together. Hamp, Milt Hinton, and myself. We was all raised up down on Rose Avenue.
What kind of kid was Milt?
Oh, he was an average kid, as I can remember. All went to school together, and played ball together a little bit. We didn't play too much with each other, at least I didn't play too much ball.
Well, you got started a little bit ahead of them, didn't you, in playing?

I guess I did, because I don't remember what become of Milt. All I remember, when I started taking violin lessons, I remember Milt's people started giving him violin lessons. Then when he moved away, I don't know what happened.
But I got started playing with these different bands while I was still living on Rose Avenue. I played (inaudible).
When did you get married?
First time I got married was 1927.
You were quite young.
Yeah.
Is that the marriage where you
had the four daughters?
Yeah.
And then you have an eight-year old son now?
He's 11.
That's by my second marriage. I've been married 20 years this time.
Really?
Uh-huh.
You were almost born married.
(Laughter.)
I had 11 months of grace -- I mean 11 years of grace in between my first and second marriages.
And you have four daughters and one son.
One son.
Raised them in music.
Yeah, well I play music.
That's a good record. Tell me some more about Tiny Parham. About how many records did you do with him?
Oh, my goodness, I don't have any idea. I did a lot of them, come to find out.
What label?
Victor. But we was recording quite a bit. Because he used to write the tunes. And about this time, used to do six sides. Sometimes eight sides. Did you ever hear of 'Head-Hunter's Dream'?
No.
That was one of the records we made.
"A Head-Hunter's Dream"?
Uh-huh.
Didn't Junie Cobb play some with him?
I can't remember. I believe so.
He's another sort of mystery man in jazz history.
Yeah.
I'm never quite sure whether he plays trumpet or tuba.
Saxophone.
Saxophone?
Yeah. He was way ahead of me.
Didn't he have a brother, also, who played?
Yeah. I can't think of his brother's name. I think his brother played trumpet.
Maybe that's who I'm thinking of.
Yeah, had a brother played trumpet.
I remember one record, great name for a band, "Junie Cobb and his Ears of Corn."
Yeah.
Well, how often would you record with Tiny Parham? You said you recorded a lot. Once a month? Couple times a month?
Several times a month, I'd say.
And the records would come out quickly in those days.
Yeah, they would come out real quick.
Well, were they played a lot on jukeboxes? I mean, what was the -- you know, the people he was aiming for?
I don't know.
Well, did he work gigs around town?
Yeah, worked steady with him at the ______, for a while, 35th and State.
Yeah? When was that?
That was first, it had to be before Earl Hines.

Yeah, must have been. A little before '29, before '30, because '29 I was in the Metropolitan Theater. I went in the Metropolitan Theater in '28. This must have been around the same time I recorded with Jelly Roll, right
around '27. Who were some of the guys that were on those recording dates with Tiny?
Omer Simeon, Shirley Clay, and -- I can't think who -- oh, Preston Jackson made some.
Were you playing tuba or string bass?

Tuba. I hadn't started on string bass yet. Tiny played piano. I'm trying to remember who played drums on that. Preston Jackson, I think, may have been on trombone. I don't remember whether Dutrey or Kid Ory was in on them records or not. Because they were doing a lot of recording with the same bands.
Did you play some with Orey?
Yeah. Played with Dutrey.
Recording or gigs?
Recording.
What was your impression of the New Orleans musicians?
Well, they was all the same to me. Yeah, we got along fine. Just like Chicago musicians. I never had any trouble with them.
Certainly recorded with a lot of fine people, played with a lot of fine people.
Uh-huh.
Do you have photographs of most of the bands you played in?
No.
You never were a collector, huh?
Never was a collector. Just like I say, I never figured, you know. Then in the moving, and the separating, and the moving going on, I lost a lot of stuff. That's the way I lost my scores.
Thus, the interview ends.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
